Because the realms of form and formlessness are stored within the collection of *śamatha*, this manas follows [the object] subtly at all times. To explain the three realms: they are the places where sentient beings return and gather.
It is like a marketplace;
in Sanskrit, it is called *āpaṇa*. [End of] Treatise.
Regarding the statement "it should be understood that this is likewise for those born in the desire realm," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 63, clarifies that it is identical to this.
Thus, that treatise says:

"In whatever place they arise, these afflictions are subsumed under that very level. This explains that wherever the seventh consciousness arises, the associated delusions are likewise subsumed under that same level.
Furthermore, the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (19) states:
If a person (pudgala) is born within this realm,

it should be known that the afflictions associated with this mind are subsumed under the essential nature of this very realm; this is the explanation of the *Yogācārabhūmi* according to the levels (*bhūmi*).

The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* relies upon the [eighteen] elements (*dhātu*); although there are slight differences regarding their coarse or subtle aspects, the general meaning is essentially the same. Thus says the treatise.
Regarding the phrase "the Arhat’s meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth":
according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 63, it does not mention the meditative attainment of cessation.
Thus, that treatise states:
For those who have abandoned desire, whether the mundane path of cultivation is present before them or not present.
These afflictions continue to manifest without interruption;
however, when the supramundane path manifests for those in training who have already seen the track, [the afflictions cease].
These afflictions cannot manifest while [one is] in that state;
however, having emerged from it, they manifest once again because of one's thorough mastery.
Because they have not been permanently severed,
if these [afflictions] do not manifest in any form whatsoever for those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa),

one should know that these afflictions are abandoned all at once and simultaneously, solely by means of abandoning desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
It is not like other afflictions that are abandoned gradually; the commentary explains that these afflictions refer to the four delusions associated with this seventh consciousness,
which differ from those treated in this treatise.
The commentary and its explanation are as set forth in the sub-commentary (*śū*).
Regarding the passage in the sub-commentary from "eighty-eight" up to "not submitting to the semblance," etc.:
6. The distinction between the six and seven afflictions:
the difference lies in their severance by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
However, neither can be suppressed by the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*).
This is called "the similarity of non-submission.
According to that treatise:
"Furthermore, one observes the time when affliction (saṃkleśa) attains liberation."
Furthermore, one is able to attain ultimate liberation from other defilements;
however, at the time one attains liberation from other defilements,
one does not thereby immediately become liberated from the defilement of various views.
Why is this? Because those born here rely on the mundane path,
up to and including the ability to abandon all craving for the sphere of nothingness.
While their minds have attained liberation from the remaining afflictions of the lower stages,
they have not yet been liberated from the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Due to this view, they do not perceive the distinction between the diverse, composite natures of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the lower and higher stages.
They universally conceptualize [the aggregates] as a self or as what belongs to a self;
due to these causes and conditions, although they may ascend to the Peak of Existence, they subsequently fall back.
By means of the supramundane path, one first abandons all views of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
subsequently, one is able to permanently abandon the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*).
Due to this causal condition, there is no longer any falling back.
Commentary:
Regarding the question, "When one reaches the point where this consciousness can also be taken as an object, it too should be abandoned," the intended meaning of this inquiry is as follows.
If it were not permitted that [the afflictions] are abandoned, it would contradict the principle [of their abandonment].
If, however, they were also called "abandoned" merely by virtue of being the objects of focus,
how could the treatise state that the lowest-of-the-low (mṛdumṛdu) afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) are abandoned all at once and simultaneously?
Since it has already been abandoned previously,
what is meant by "abandoning all at once"?
Commentary:
When one understands the reality through this analogy,
there is no longer any fruit brought about by evil karma;
the eighth [verse] states "except."
The afflictions of the bhāvanāmārga still remain;
the grasping at a self has not yet perished.

Since the seventh [consciousness] that can serve as an object-condition has not been severed, it cannot be said to be abandoned. Question: In the darśanamārga, there is merely the absence of one portion of the eighth [consciousness]; thus, the eighth is said to be "abandoned."

Furthermore, one part of the grasper—the seventh [consciousness]—is also deficient; thus, the seventh should be abandoned. Answer: Since the cause is lost, the effect perishes; thus, the eighth may be abandoned.
However, the seventh is not summoned by karma, and its grasping essence is not non-existent.
How can it be called equanimity?
The commentary states: "In this case, we do not rely upon that."
Regarding the statement "it also extends to the untainted (anāsrava)":
although the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* both state that pure consciousness exists in the stage of Buddhahood,
neither the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* nor the treatise by Asaṅga mentions its existence.
For this reason, one should not take later treatises as authoritative proof.
Regarding the statement in the *Xianyang lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the Holy Teachings), "up to the practice of equanimity," etc.:
According to that treatise, it says:
"The 'mental consciousness' (manas) refers to that which arises from the seeds of the ālayavijñāna and, in turn, takes that very consciousness as its object;
it is associated with self-delusion, self-love, the grasping at 'I' and 'mine,' and self-pride."
Alternatively, it may be the opposite of that association:
at all times, its activity consists of relying on and uplifting [the mind],
or it functions equally with that [mind] as its nature of discerning.
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "the consciousnesses cited [in the sūtras] extend up to the storehouse consciousness," this is stated according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
which speaks of the storehouse consciousness as being either two-fold or three-fold.

Therefore, this treatise does not discuss the state beyond training (aśaikṣa), because those beyond training lack the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna). One interpretation holds that it was not mentioned due to brevity; however, a detailed examination shows that it is not for the sake of brevity.
This is raised as an objection based on the number of consciousnesses arising as set forth in the *Mahā-śāstra*.
Since the root treatise (*Mūla-śāstra*) cites the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) as the subject under discussion,
this objection cannot be leveled against those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Therefore, the commentary is correct.
If one does not adopt that text as the underlying principle,
then raising an objection against the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is harmless.
Commentary:
Regarding the eighth point, "as with the other seven consciousnesses," the question is:
according to the previous master’s own admission, the sixth consciousness of one in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) on the Noble Path is without support.

If the nature of consciousness arises through transformation, does this not constitute an indeterminate offense against others? Answer: Within the co-existent supports (sahabhū-āśraya), there are both common and uncommon factors;
such is the case for the sixth mental consciousness during states such as the Noble Path (āryamārga).
The opponent also admits the existence of simultaneous mutual supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*).
Since this is not specifically excluded within the subject of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), there is no fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).
[Commentary:]
If one establishes the aforementioned general thesis that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) has no support,
some scholars object: "The mental consciousness of the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-mārga) and that of noble beings (ārya) are both included within the subject of the proposition (dharmin)."
How could there be an "inconclusive" [reason] within the subject (*dharmin*) of a given school (*siddhānta*)? To explain in detail:
regarding the five types of inconclusive reasons (*anaikāntika-hetu*), they depend upon two kinds of examples (*dṛṣṭānta*);
that which does not exist in either of them, serving as the locus where the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is absent, constitutes the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Although the proponent establishes [the argument] with the intention that the noble path and so forth exist within the subject (*dharmin*),
he subsequently states the thesis that the noble one’s intention is not existent;
from the perspective of logic, this ought to reside in a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
Since the reason (*hetu*) is already present in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), why would it not be indeterminate (*anaikāntika*)?
With respect to what property-possessor (*dharmin*) would it fail to be determinate?
If it is said that [the reason] was previously established within the subject (*dharmin*),
how can it then be said to be a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)?
This, too, is not problematic.
Previously, based on the general formulation, it was stated that "the subject (dharmin) is included [in the similar class].
However, according to the underlying principle, it ought to reside in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa).
This is also like the ancient formulation where the thesis and the reason were said to be contradictory.
Regarding the argument "Sound is eternal because everything is impermanent," Dharmakīrti correctly states that "because everything is impermanent" is actually the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
This is not a valid reason.

Since he has already used the correct cause (*saddhetu*) as an analogy based on principle, what loss is there now in using the correct thesis (*siddhānta*) as a point of distinction based on principle? Furthermore, the *Hetuprakaraṇa* states:

Regarding the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*): if, in a certain case, that which is to be established is said to be absent—meaning that in a locus other than the one where the probandum is excluded, the probandum itself is simply absent—that is the "dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya*) of the thesis.
Since there is nothing established as distinct regarding the noble path and so forth,
what fault is there? If it were otherwise,
then the statement that these categories encompass all established phenomena would be incomplete.
If one stops short of eliminating excesses without pursuing them to their conclusion, various errors will arise.
For this reason, the judgment in the *Śāstra* (the *Vyākhyā*) is logically certainly without contradiction.
The *Śāstra*.
If it is held that there are only six consciousnesses and no seventh,
another school objects, stating:
"The distinct doctrine [of this school] contradicts inference (anumāna), as previously noted regarding the former doctrine."
Because there is no lack of certainty (*anaikāntika*), it constitutes a semblance of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*).
The external inference has no fault regarding its members as previously stated;
the reason (*hetu*) is: "because it is subsumed under the sixth consciousness."
Just as with the sixth consciousness of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and so forth,

would an opponent not then raise the fallacy of "indefiniteness" (*anaikāntika*) by claiming that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and pseudo-cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) are [both] included within the six consciousnesses?
If that external measure takes the cause of valid cognition as its reason, it claims they are subsumed under the six consciousnesses.
There is also the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This is precisely the "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*);
how then can it be said that there is the fault of being conclusive (*niścita*)?
The intent of this refutation is as follows:
Both the preceding and succeeding positions possess the constituent members [of a valid syllogism] that lead to contradictory certainty (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
Now, the reason "being subsumed within the six consciousnesses" in the former argument has already committed the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, the specific thesis established [by the opponent] contradicts the textual passage of inference (*anumāna*) and thus lacks [a necessary member].
Later, the [opponent's] school cites that sixth member, the "reason" (*hetu*), whereby it becomes complete. Thus, there is a distinction between being deficient and not being deficient.
By what reasoning can a "contradictory certainty" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) be established?
If the opponent likewise accepts the former reason,
it is subsumed under the category of the "inconclusive through commonality" (sādhāraṇānaikāntika).
How does this constitute the sixth indeterminate fallacy (*anaikāntika*)? To explain in detail:
while it is true that the *Śū-wén* (Commentary) contains this error upon direct inspection, the primary intent of the treatise and its commentary is to rectify the reason (*hetu*).
This is a brief statement regarding the preceding causes.
Since the *Yideng* (Lamp of Meaning) is correct, there is no error in the *Shu* (Commentary).
[End of] *Shu*.
This is the first fundamental stage:
the state in which the seventh [consciousness], the grasping at a self, first does not arise.

It cannot be said that they mutually abandon one another.

One cannot cause [the eighth] to be abandoned by making it identical to the seven, nor can one abandon it by making the seven identical to the eighth. Why is this not possible? The answer is: because of the fault of defilement.
"Temporary cessation is called relinquishment (*tyāga*).
The permanent absence of other bonds regarding pure phenomena is called relinquishment.
Regarding the commentary's statement, "If it were definitively so, then one would reach the fruit of the contemplation of non-dharmas":
The intent of this objection is as follows:
If one were to definitively grant that both the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*) and its fruit are equal,
then from the eighth stage onward, there would never be a time when there is no contemplation of phenomena or its fruit.
One should therefore constantly give rise to the wisdom of equanimity.
Commentary:
Based on this, one should explain the proximate fruit.
The intent of this response is as follows:
although both types of subsequently attained wisdom are termed "fruits," they differ in terms of their proximity [to the ultimate].
Therefore, the wisdom of equality does not arise constantly.
[Commentary:
Alternatively, it is not problematic that non-conceptual wisdom exists from the eighth stage onward.
This is the second interpretation:
the two fundamental wisdoms each enter their respective two contemplations,
and the two subsequently attained wisdoms are each designated as "fruits" in relation to their own respective fundamental wisdoms.
Commentary:
If one proceeds according to the latter meaning, which treats the fruit as a complete whole,
then the fruit of dharma-emptiness is simply the arising of equanimity.
Furthermore, it does not depart from its fruit by going far away;
therefore, it is called the "Complete Treatise" (Quánlùn).
— Commentary.

That is to say, one benefits sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
The ten [virtues] attract and gather wholesome qualities;
through the merit of giving and ethical discipline, they attract the ripening of happiness such as rebirth in the heavens.
Eleventh is the goodness of the antidote,
which refers to the antidotes such as the "antidote of repudiation" that counteract the two obscurations.
Twelfth is the goodness of tranquility.
This refers to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling through the permanent abandonment of afflictions, as well as the realm of nirvana with remainder and so forth.
Thirteen types are wholesome by outflow,
namely those attained by one who has already realized tranquility.
By the power of this predominance, one gives rise to superior qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which are common or uncommon to both the mundane and supramundane realms.
[Commentary:
Regarding the twelve unwholesome [factors]:
According to that fourth [chapter], it says:
First, intrinsic unwholesomeness,
which refers to that which is bound to the desire realm and does not arise spontaneously.
And all afflictions that arise spontaneously and are capable of inciting unwholesome conduct constitute the second type:
"associated unwholesomeness," namely those factors associated with these very afflictions and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Third, non-virtue that follows along,
which refers to its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Fourth, non-virtue that initiates.
That is to say, the bodily and vocal actions produced by those [afflictions] are the five types of ultimate unwholesomeness;
that is, all cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Sixth is innate unwholesomeness (*upapatti-lābhika-akuśala*),
which arises spontaneously through habitual practice without depending on deliberate reflection.
Seventh is unwholesomeness of application (*prayoga-akuśala*).
It arises from associating with unwholesome friends and improper reflection.
Eighth, it consists of making offerings to the unwholesome,
taking refuge in opposition [to the Triple Gem], and killing for the sake of a single class of celestial beings.
The ninth is harmful unwholesomeness, which refers to the performance of various wrong actions of body,
speech, and mind in all circumstances, such as establishing shrines and engaging in acts of worship based on false views.
Tenth, that which induces non-virtue:
the performance of the three types of unwholesome karma induces undesirable maturation (*vipāka*).
Eleventh, that which is the antithesis of virtue: non-virtue.
This refers to the factors that are the objects of opposition for their respective remedies; namely,
the twelve obstructive unwholesome states,
which are the factors capable of obstructing all categories of wholesome qualities.
Regarding "the fourteen indeterminate [factors] such as the calculation of the assembly," the commentary states:
"The fourteen indeterminate [factors]."
According to that fourth [chapter], it says:
First is the indeterminate by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).

This refers to the eight bases of form (*rūpa-dhātu-āyatana*), the mental concomitants (*citta-samprayukta*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and the groups of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*).
The second is the indeterminate associated with [the name],
which refers to all names and so forth,
as well as the mind and mental factors subsumed under those names and so forth, when they are accompanied by a mind that is neither defiled nor pure.
Third, the non-defined [state] of persistence,
which refers to the habitual tendencies of that conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Fourth, the non-defined [state] of origination.
This refers to the bodily and vocal actions produced by those minds and mental factors that are subsumed therein.
There are five types of ultimate indeterminate (paramārtha-avyākṛta):
namely, space (ākāśa) and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Six are acquired at birth and are neutral (*avyākṛta*):
namely, all unwholesome states, wholesome states with outflows (*sāsrava*), and the maturation (*vipāka*) thereof.
Seven are neutral by way of application (*prayoga*).
This refers to the deportment and the spheres of craftsmanship belonging to one whose mind is neither defiled nor virtuous;
it also refers to the eight types of present offerings that are indeterminate.
For example, there may be someone who, with the perception of a deity, takes refuge in a certain class of celestial beings, remaining free from the intent to kill and from wrong views.
Furthermore, establishing shrines and temples and engaging in acts of making offerings causes immeasurable multitudes to neither produce merit nor demerit at such places;
this is the ninth type of indeterminate action that benefits others.
That is to say, there is someone who practices giving toward their own servants, wife, children,
and so forth, with a mind that is neither defiled nor pure;
this constitutes ten types of indeterminate enjoyment.
This refers, for example, to someone who uses material requisites with a mind that is free from affliction through immediate discernment;
this constitutes eleven types of attraction of the indeterminate.
This refers, for example, to someone who, due to habitual practice, engages in a craft or skillful art.
In future lives, they will again draw forth a body with such characteristics;
by means of this body, they will master the fields of arts and crafts,
reaching their ultimate perfection with great speed.
The twelfth is the indeterminate [action] as an antidote.
This refers, for example, to someone who, in order to treat an illness and attain well-being,
takes medicine with a mind of careful discernment.
Thirteenth is the tranquil indeterminate,
which refers to the various afflictions and so forth of the form and formless realms;
they are so called because they are suppressed and concealed by śamatha.
The fourteenth [type] is the neutral (avyākṛta) outflow (*niṣyanda*), which refers to dharmas such as those associated with transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and those that are co-existent;
these are termed the "concomitant class" (*sahaja-varga*). This mind and its mental factors are neutral because they initiate transformations for the sake of sport (*krīḍā*).
If it is for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, one should know that it is wholesome.
Commentary:
The five consciousnesses cannot transform the mind to initiate karma.
According to that treatise, it says:

"The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, are said to follow the mental consciousness in its transformation; they follow it in its transformation into states that are wholesome or defiled."
"Following the movement of the karma-initiating mind. The commentary explains:
"It follows the will to produce and follows the will to engage in wholesome, defiled, pure, or tainted states.
The five consciousnesses merely follow the movement of the karma-initiating mind; they do not move independently."
"Initiating" (*pravartaka*) refers to the arousal [of action]; it is the mind that, as the causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*), gives rise to karma.
"Conforming" (*anuvartaka*) refers to that which arises following the force of the aforementioned initiating karma.

Regarding the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*’s statement that the six consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously with the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), there is one interpretation which holds that they are not coexistent.
According to the Yogācāra commentators, there are generally three interpretations.
One states that the five consciousnesses exist for only a single moment,
and furthermore, they do not arise simultaneously.
The second [master] says that although the five acquisitions arise simultaneously in a single moment;
the third says that the five acquisitions arise simultaneously over multiple moments.
All three, however, do not allow for the five [acquisitions] to be of three different natures (trividha) simultaneously.
There is an interpretation in the *Vyākhyā* that relies solely on the first objection.
Now, I shall provide a separate explanation:
here, we rely only on the second point stated, namely that the five natures do not coexist.
Why is this so? Furthermore, throughout this treatise, from beginning to end, there is no mention of the five [factors] not arising simultaneously.
Moreover, the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts state:
If the five consciousnesses arise, then seven [mental factors] function simultaneously.
Such passages are understood by all masters.
How, then, can it be said that the five consciousnesses do not function simultaneously?
Furthermore, this very text states that the arising of wholesome or defiled visual consciousness and so forth must necessarily be induced by the mental consciousness (*manas*).
Since it is accepted that the five [sensory] consciousnesses are simultaneous, it should likewise be the case for the sixth;
thus, it is clearly understood that the co-arising of the five consciousnesses is indeed admitted.
Furthermore, the second objection is that the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness,
which are either impulsive (*ābhoga*) or resultant (*niṣyanda*), may arise together in varying numbers.
If the first master does not allow for their simultaneous arising, [then...]
Why is the second [point] formulated as such an objection? To explain in detail:

since there is no specific scriptural teaching [to the contrary] and the underlying principle is universally applicable, one cannot justify resorting to scripture to refute a broad interpretation; the reason for this is as follows.
Is it that the three meanings accepted by the Yogācāra commentators are not admitted [by you]?
If they are not admitted, what does this imply?
If they are indeed admitted, for what reason are they not stated in the commentary?
Because it accords with the foremost [teaching].
Furthermore, this treatise states:

"The *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts explain that the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) associated with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise simultaneously, based upon multiple moments (*kṣaṇa*), and so forth."
Is this not a simultaneous realization of both the three natures and the coexistence of all consciousnesses?
If one were to say that it is only a realization of the coexistence of the three natures,
that too would be unreasonable.
The treatise states: "Nature and co-existence both depend on the convergence of multiple moments.
What fault is there in that consciousness also being present during that convergence of multiple moments?
Both nature and the co-existence of consciousness are established in that treatise.
Whether it is appropriate or not,
why such uncertainty?
Suppose this text were intended solely to accord with the three natures (trisvabhāva).
Applying this principle to consciousness (*vijñāna*) is likewise not contradictory;
moreover, the meaning within the text applies to both the nature (*prakṛti*) and consciousness.
Furthermore, the treatise does not state that the five consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously as a proof for the [commentary’s] refutation.
Where does this treatise state that the five consciousnesses are simultaneous and last for only a single moment?
It refers to the second [chapter].
Furthermore, the treatise merely states that the five [consciousnesses] are rendered wholesome or defiled by being led by the mental consciousness (*manas*).

By what reasoning is it proven that [the mental consciousness] arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses? If the five consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, would that not obstruct the drawing forth [of the object] by the mind?
If one were to argue that because the text mentions "the five consciousnesses," it thereby proves they are simultaneous, [that would be a fallacy].
Likewise, the five consciousnesses should also be non-simultaneous; this is because they are referred to as "the five consciousnesses.
Next, it says that the sixth [consciousness] penetrates all three natures.
This is a refutation based on the opponent's own position;
it does not refute the sixth [consciousness] by admitting the five [sensory consciousnesses] as co-arising.
Furthermore, the later master’s objection states that they may indeed co-arise.

This demonstrates that the five consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously at all times; by using the term "possible" (*yō*) instead of "always co-arising," it distinguishes this from the constant co-occurrence [of the mental consciousness].
It does not mean that the former master admitted the simultaneous arising of the five [consciousnesses] when he used the phrase "possible co-occurrence."
Thus, there is no contradiction between this commentary and the underlying principles. The commentary states:
"From the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, chapter nineteen, up to 'the innate ear,' [it refers to] the discernment of the determined object, and so forth."
This is the first cause; from this, the ear-consciousness arises simultaneously.
This is the second cause, which demonstrates that the concentrated mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to take both concentrated objects and non-concentrated objects as its cognitive domain.
Therefore, the phrase "various objects of focus" is spoken;
these are the dharmāyatana as the object of meditative concentration. Regarding "various objects":

The treatise states: "There is an interpretation that they arise together with the five sense objects. This means that [the mental consciousness] can arise simultaneously with the [five sensory consciousnesses].
Regarding "more or less sparse," there are two interpretations:
the first is based on the quantity of mindfulness,
and the second is based on the quantity of consciousness.
There are many obstacles and difficulties, as fully explained in the *Pradīpa*.
Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that [the text] was only produced at a later time:
According to that treatise, it states:
"It is not the mental consciousness associated with that very meditative absorption," yet there is no word "only" (唯).
The meanings of "only" (*wei*) and "immediately" (*ji*) are slightly similar.
The intent of this treatise is to demonstrate that one does not grasp [the object] solely through the mind;
thus, it changes "immediately" to "only."
Furthermore, there is no character "ya" [in the root text].
Moreover, the commentary states: "This refers to a practitioner," which is also an intentional addition.
The rest of the text is identical.
Commentary:
If one encounters the condition of sound, that is precisely auditory consciousness.
There are two interpretations regarding the *Vyākhyā-śāstra*.
I shall now explain them separately.
"Arising from meditative concentration" refers to the arising of a distracted mind after emerging from concentration. A detailed examination states:
This may also be the case. However,
since the treatise states that one subsequently emerges from meditative absorption, the arising [of the thought] must pertain to being within meditative absorption.
Regarding the phrase "the intention arises": the meaning of *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) is profound and far-reaching. Regarding the commentary:
"When the distracted mind enters into equanimity (*upekṣā*)."
This answers the preceding question.
There are two general interpretations:
if one enters the state of equanimity with a distracted mind, [the sound] will certainly not reach the ear.
This is the first interpretation.
Although the second interpretation also allows for differences even when reaching that very nature,
this is the second interpretation.
Regarding the first interpretation, there are again two meanings:
first, entering the meditative absorption of equanimity;
second, initially arising from that absorption.
"Arising from meditative concentration" refers to the moment just before emerging from concentration.
During these two moments, the mental consciousness and the auditory consciousness share the same object.
(Commentary)
Regarding the sixty-ninth statement concerning the existence of transformations (*nirmāṇa*) and so forth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
it is fully explained as in the *Dīpa-vibhaṅga*.
[End of] Commentary.
Regarding the statement that the four consciousnesses take postures (*īryāpatha*) and so forth as their objects, there are briefly three explanations.
First, because those postures mostly depend upon roads, they receive the name "road. One explanation states that posture is itself informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*).

The essence of the pathways (*patha*) consists of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Because these four elements are that upon which deportment (*īryāpatha*) relies, they are called the "pathways of deportment. Second, it is said that the four great elements constitute the nature of deportment;
that which gives rise to those [deportmental] minds is termed the "pathway."
Because they serve as its basis,
both are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds. Third, the four types of sensory objects are collectively termed "dignified deportment" (*airyāpathika*),
because they are inseparable from the matter of dignified deportment.
That upon which this mind relies is called the "path" (*mārga*);
this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

The minds that take those modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) as their objects are all *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds. Regarding the "spheres of craftsmanship" (*śailpasthānika*), there are likewise three types of explanations.
Because those crafts are designated based on their various locations, they receive the designation "locations. One explanation states that "crafts" refers to the two [faculties] of body and speech.
The craft of the body has as its essence the informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) of long, short, and so forth, such as the construction of palaces and the like.
The basis is derived matter,
having as its nature the primary elements of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility;
it consists of skill in speech, song, and so forth.
The essence [of this faculty] is the sound itself that is produced.

Its locus consists of the five sense objects upon which songs and so forth depend; according to another view, it consists of four sense objects. These five sense objects are termed "crafts" (*śailpasthānika*).
That which can give rise to those [mental] states is called a "basis" (*āyatana*), because it serves as their support.
Both [the first two cases] are *tatpuruṣa* compounds. The third case states that craftsmanship itself is called a "basis."
Because the four and five sense objects are what the mind relies upon,

they are designated by the *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) interpretation; as for the mind directed toward the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), all such instances are explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) interpretation.
